learningGoal: Understand how to structure a test so that setup, behavior, and verification are easy to reason about.
whyNow: This demo lesson will be replaced by the next verified lesson generated by the daily cron. It exists only to exercise the live dashboard before the first lab run.
known: Arrange–Act–Assert is a common organization pattern for tests.
inference: Separating phases can make a failing Tregu test easier to diagnose.
uncertainty: A well-organized test can still assert the wrong expected behavior.
test: Read one test in the 383 repository and identify its Arrange, Act, and Assert sections.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A test should answer one focused question. First prepare the situation, then perform the behavior, then check the result. The pattern is useful because it makes the test's story visible to another engineer.

sections.title: Why it matters in 383
sections.body: A market deadline decision should be testable separately from authentication, database writes, UI rendering, and email delivery. Small boundaries make failures informative instead of mysterious.

example.explanation: The inputs are arranged first, the comparison is the act, and the assertion checks the boundary case.

diagram.source:
flowchart LR

  B --> C[Assert result]
  C --> D[Trust one behavior]
diagram.caption: A small test protects one clear behavior.

quiz.question: What belongs in Arrange?
quiz.explanation: Arrange prepares the situation before the behavior runs.

quiz.question: Why include an exact-deadline case?
quiz.explanation: Equality at a boundary often exposes > versus >= mistakes.

quiz.question: What is the Act phase?
quiz.explanation: Act performs the behavior under test.
